## Every published model

The paper's models were fit in Stata, and several of them were never in the original R code: the R file had exploratory models only. The replication fits every model the paper and its supplement report, as they are presented (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026):

| Table | Blocks | Outcome and exposure |
|---|---|---|
| Table 2 | With and without albumin and hemoglobin; without HSAs with 0 facilities | Early start, density category |
| eTable 1 | Black and White individuals | Early start, density category |
| eTable 2 | With and without albumin and hemoglobin; albumin and hemoglobin multiply imputed; Black and White individuals | Early start, continuous density |
| eTable 3 | With albumin and hemoglobin; without HSAs with 0 facilities | eGFR (linear), density category |

Each block has Models 1 to 3. The models are listed in one table, one row per published column, so nothing reported is missed and a model that appears in two blocks (Model 1 in both blocks of Table 2) is fit once. Model 1 never includes albumin or hemoglobin and uses all patients of its group, as in Table 2, where it is identical in both blocks. Within a race group, race is not a covariate. The eTable 1 headings disagree on whether albumin and hemoglobin are included (see the [supplement](supplement.qmd)); both of its sample sizes match the complete-case models, so they are included.

```{r}
#| label: define-published-models
#| eval: false
```

## Models

Mixed-effects models with a random intercept for HSA, progressively adjusted, fit with `glmmTMB` [@glmmtmb]: logistic for early start, linear for eGFR. With albumin and hemoglobin, patients missing either value drop out of Models 2 and 3, as in the paper's complete-case models. The covariates follow the paper's Table 2 footnotes; the "HSA quality benchmarks" in Model 3 are the three the paper's Methods name (HbA1c testing and eye examinations among enrollees with diabetes, and ambulatory-sensitive discharges).

### Choosing the model-fitting package

The paper fit its models in Stata 15, whose default for these models is adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature with 7 points. In R there are several ways to fit the same model. On synthetic data shaped like Model 3 (4,000 patients, 60 HSAs, about 40 covariate terms), they compared as follows:

| Fit | Time | Convergence warnings | Odds ratio, highest vs zero density |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lme4::glmer` [@lme4_pkg], default settings | 117 s | 4 | 10.08 (not converged) |
| `lme4::glmer`, rescaled covariates, higher iteration limit | 111 s | 0 | 10.62 |
| `lme4::glmer`, 7-point quadrature (Stata's default) | 119 s | 0 | 10.63 |
| `glmmTMB` [@glmmtmb] | 4 s | 0 | 10.63 |

The numbers are synthetic; only the comparison matters. `glmmTMB` gave the same estimates as a fully converged `glmer` in about a thirtieth of the time, without rescaling, and quadrature with 7 points rather than the Laplace approximation changed the odds ratios only in the third decimal, because each HSA has many patients. The analysis therefore uses `glmmTMB` (decided by Vagish Hemmige, 27 October 2026). Two other options were considered:

-   **`GLMMadaptive`** fits the model with adaptive quadrature and any number of points, closest to Stata's method, but is slower on data of this size.
-   **`MixedModels.jl`**, the Julia successor to `lme4` by its original author, is the fastest for very large models and can be called from R with the `jlme` package [@jlme]. It needs a Julia installation, and `jlme` is a young, single-maintainer package with little recent activity, so it was not used.

## Multiple imputation

The paper reports multiple imputation of albumin and hemoglobin by chained equations with 10 imputations (eTable 2), done in Stata; it gives no other detail, and the original R code has none. Here only albumin and hemoglobin are imputed, by predictive mean matching (the `mice` default for numeric variables), from the outcome, the density category and the Model 3 covariates. HSA is not a predictor (about 3,400 levels), and continuous density is not used as a predictor because it duplicates the density category. This imputation model awaits the deciders' confirmation ([#D7]).
